title: The Relentless Pursuit of “Equal”: Integrating LSU
subtitle: Oral histories of civil rights at LSU and in Baton Rouge
credit: T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History and LSU Libraries Special Collections. Curated by Leah Wood Jewett, Barry Cowan and Jennifer A. Cramer.
intro:
The Relentless Pursuit of “Equal” traces the evolution of LSU from an institution embracing an official policy of racial segregation to one actively promoting the concept that “cultural inclusion at LSU is paramount to the success of the university.”

Oral history clips from those who integrated LSU sit beside timelines of the 1953 Baton Rouge bus boycott and of civil rights activities in East Baton Rouge from the 1920s through the 1970s, in the voices of those who lived them.
physical_note: Shown in the Hill Memorial Library Lecture Hall from January 21 to March 29, 2014, for the 50th anniversary of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

blocks.body: The exhibition’s four galleries side by side, from Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 to the building LSU named for A. P. Tureaud, Sr., in 1990: the suits and students who integrated LSU, the 1953 bus boycott, civil rights in East Baton Rouge, and the nation.

pages.title: Integrating LSU
pages.lead_caption: A. P. Tureaud, Jr., and his father, his attorney in the suit, waiting in the LSU registrar’s office. Newspaper photo, 1953.

blocks.body: LSU was integrated one school at a time, through separate suits for the law school, the graduate school and the undergraduate college. Many of the cases were argued by A. P. Tureaud, Sr.
Army veteran Charles J. Hatfield, III, files suit to attend LSU Law School.
Southern University Law School opens and Hatfield’s case is dismissed as a result.

blocks.title: Leander Perez at the deposition
blocks.credit: A. P. Tureaud, Jr., LSU alumnus
blocks.transcript:
Yes, I remember that deposition very . . . I remember the one that I went to very well. I went with my father, and I think it was Bob Carter. The thing that I remembered most about it, because I didn’t quite know what to expect—I’d never been to a deposition before—was the presentation that Leander Perez made. My mother went. My mother went, I remember that now. Leander Perez, in either summarizing some information or whatever . . . He was very colorful. He was dressed in a sort of a plantation beige outfit with a sort of a string tie, or whatever. He was a very colorful character and used a lot of flamboyant language. Was very dramatic and also could be very cruel and biting and sarcastic. He was known around New Orleans and around Louisiana for his hatred, hatred of black people and mistreatment of the people that worked for him or worked for his family and all that kind of stuff.

One statement that he made that I’ll never forget, because this was a long time ago, was . . . He pointed to me and walked in my direction and looked right dead at me and said that, “There sits the only ungrateful nigra in the state of Louisiana. Because we have gone to great expense and trouble to build up fine black universities in this state. Why is Mr. Tureaud not willing to avail himself of this opportunity?” He said it with such sarcasm and with such belief. It was just very intimidating and I . . . It made me angry.

blocks.body: Roy Samuel Wilson successfully sues to attend LSU Law School. He does not complete the program. He was represented by attorney A. P. Tureaud, Sr. Here, A. P. Tureaud, Jr., recalls his father’s relationships with the students he represented.

blocks.title: More than just their lawyer
blocks.credit: A. P. Tureaud, Jr., LSU alumnus, interviewed by Rachel Emanuel-Wallace
blocks.transcript:
RACHEL EMANUEL-WALLACE: Were you aware of, once these students were enrolled, of their contact with your father [A. P. Tureaud, Sr.] on what . . . how things were going for them?

A. P. TUREAUD, JR.: Oh yes, he constantly maintained contact with them [Roy Wilson, Daryle Foister, and Lutrill Payne]. He would also drive up to the campus if they were having problems of one kind or another and needed support. He was more than . . . more than just their lawyer. He was like a support system. In some ways, without sounding mushy, he was really like a parent supporting their kid in an environment or young person in an environment. Because a lot of those graduate students were well into their adulthood, they weren’t right out of high school. He was very supportive.

blocks.title: LSU Law Admits Collins and Morial

blocks.caption: Ernest “Dutch” Morial, later mayor of New Orleans.

blocks.body: Robert Collins and Ernest “Dutch” Morial enroll in LSU Law School.

blocks.title: The first Black law students
blocks.credit: Ernest “Dutch” Morial, LSU alumnus, interviewed by Nina Pugh
blocks.transcript:
ERNEST “DUTCH” MORIAL: I guess it was a kind of different experience for us and for me. We were the first black graduates, first black law students. Except that the year before we entered in 1951, Roy Wilson had been there as a student for a short time under the United States Supreme Court-ordered desegregation of the law school.

NINA PUGH: Well, I know that in addition to your many distinctions you have the distinction of being the first black graduate of law school. What was it like being a pioneer, in a manner of speaking, at LSU law school?

MORIAL: Well, I think that generally there was not a great deal of hostility to . . . in my opinion. There were some who shunned myself and [Robert] Collins, I guess. Some were cordial. They would speak to you when they were alone, but when they were with a group they might not say anything to you, because I guess they were fearful of being criticized by some of their white peers. And of course, we couldn’t use . . . You know, we couldn’t go in the facilities in Tiger Town. They were just off limits. The blacks couldn’t go in there.

PUGH: How did you feel that the faculty . . . law faculty regarded the change of events?

MORIAL: Well, I think the faculty accepted. I think [Dean Henry] McMahon was . . . I remember registration. I think he was very cordial, you know, friendly and told us that we were going to be treated like any other law student. I think that was the way it was by the faculty. I didn’t sense any overt or evidences of discrimination on the part of the faculty. If it was present, they didn’t manifest it.

blocks.caption: Telegram from L. A. Payne to Pearl Payne, June 14, 1951: “Registration completed all is well.”

blocks.body: Lutrill Payne successfully files suit to attend LSU Graduate School.

blocks.title: The first credit from the graduate school
blocks.credit: Pearl Payne, interviewed by Jennifer Abraham
blocks.transcript:
PEARL PAYNE: So [A. P.] Tureaud, Jr., when he went down there . . . He said that you couldn’t study. He said they took turns beating on the walls at night. And there . . . He had been an A student down in New Orleans. He said . . . So he just couldn’t study. He said every time his daddy would bring him back [to campus] on Saturdays, it was just like he said, carrying him to the penitentiary. Bring him back on Sunday and come get him on Friday evening, he said. Because they just wouldn’t permit him to study. They just annoyed him.

But now, like with [Lutrill] Payne, Payne said he had no trouble with them. He said sometimes in the dining area, you went in there to eat, he said there were certain students that would sit there and talk with you. Because we had some from here that he knew. Then he said when he went in, if it was just a vacant table, said he just sat there. He wasn’t looking for company and he just sat there. So he said he really didn’t have any problem with any of them. Just like when I went down there, which was year later, fifty-one, two, fifty-three, before I went and graduated in fifty-six. Well, I had no problem with them. Even the girls of the white race, they even studied with us. So we had no problem whatever.

JENNIFER ABRAHAM: And you were in graduate school, too. So there’s a little bit of a more mature . . .

PAYNE: [agrees] Yes, more mature group.

ABRAHAM: So you got a letter saying, “You’re accepted . . .”

PAYNE: You saw that didn’t you? Well, that’s when we sent the picture. In this letter that’s in this book, they said they were sorry but LSU was whites only. See, they didn’t know. When he said he was an agriculture teacher in the state of Louisiana and that he wanted to come there because it would kind of enhance his . . . be more at home with what he’s going to expect. So when they sent that, well, then that’s when the lawyers got busy, you know, saying that we just have to, you know file suit.

ABRAHAM: And who were your lawyers?

PAYNE: [A. P.] Tureaud [Sr.]

ABRAHAM: And did Thurgood Marshall assist him?

PAYNE: Thurgood Marshall assisted him.

ABRAHAM: So tell me about them. Tell me about what you remember about them.

PAYNE: Well, I tell you what they would do. They would visit our home and they would find out things about how things were going. And they were pressing those suits, you know, to do that. So it was a matter . . . They knew what to do to get these schools open because they knew it was only fair to do that. So they won every case they had. They were able to win their cases. And he just went down there; Payne was just such a person . . . Brave, I guess I wouldn’t have been as brave. But he just got in his car and drove on down, you know, when it was time for the trial.

ABRAHAM: So he [the judge] ordered Payne to be admitted to LSU Grad School and he was the first African American admitted to the graduate school.

PAYNE: That’s right. And to receive credit in the graduate school. He was the first African American to receive credit from the graduate school.

blocks.body: Charles E. Harrington graduates from LSU with a master’s degree in education.

blocks.caption: Newspaper report of Daryle E. Foister’s admission.

blocks.body: Former army nurse Daryle E. Foister successfully sues to enroll in LSU Medical School’s Nursing Program.

blocks.caption: A. P. Tureaud, Jr., and his father, his attorney in the suit, waiting in the LSU registrar’s office. Newspaper photo, 1953.

blocks.body: A. P. Tureaud, Jr., successfully sues to enroll at LSU as an undergraduate. He later transfers to Xavier University.

blocks.title: It was like I didn’t exist
blocks.credit: A. P. Tureaud, Jr., LSU alumnus, interviewed by Rachel Emanuel-Wallace
blocks.transcript:
The professors were . . . It was like I didn’t exist. One woman was particularly awful. She was an older woman. She announced my first day that . . . not to me, she never . . . People talked about me as though, as I said, I was an inanimate object. She said to her class this was the first time she had ever taught a nigra. [chuckles] I was shocked. And she just didn’t know how she was going to get through this experience. She taught me math. Nobody sat near me. The kids sat all around me. If I sat in the corner, they would move to the opposite side of the room. If I sat in the middle, they would move to the sides. I never sat in the same place or whatever. But it . . . You were just playing head trips all the time. You were trying to figure out how you were going to make today work. It got to be very, very lonely and depressing.

We were playing racquetball and you had to have a partner. I remember this guy . . . If they didn’t . . . If the professor or the teacher didn’t mention my name, many of them didn’t know who I was because there were a lot of international students at LSU, and many of them looked more swarthy than I did. Of course, with your hair all shaved off you couldn’t tell too much anyway. I remember this guy standing next to me saying, “I’ve been looking around here waiting for that nigger to come in and I don’t see him. I hope I don’t get him as my partner. My friends will give me a hard time.” I said, “Well, there’re a few niggers here, but they’re not black.” He didn’t know what I was talking about. [Tureaud and Wallace laugh] He ended up getting me, and I don’t know if he ever heard the name. I didn’t . . . I wasn’t going to say, “Well, I’m the black person here.” I just thought, “Goodness gracious, how long is it going to take for this to . . . for them to get over this thing?” . . .

I particularly remember the women who worked in the cafeteria where I ate. They were very quiet, but they were very supportive. They would smile or wink at you. Some of them would actually come up and say, “We’re very happy you’re here.” But quietly, they didn’t want any of the white staff to hear it or the white kids to hear it, I guess . . . But they were proud and very supportive.

My most touching moment—I don’t know if I can say this because it chokes me up but—my most touching moment at LSU, and I’ll never forget it was . . . this . . . I told you . . . I mentioned this to you once before. One morning, I came out . . . I couldn’t sleep and I came out just to be outside and to get away from that crazy dormitory with all the noise and stuff. It was like six o’clock in the morning, and I was coming out of the dorm. I don’t know where I was going, but there was this black man out there sitting in a truck. He had on bib overalls and he had a little boy with him. As I came out the entrance, he walked over to me and . . . big smile on his face and he said . . . He asked me if I was A. P. Tureaud. I said, “Yes.” He said, “I thought you were.” He said that he had been to the campus a few times, but he hadn’t seen me. He lived somewhere in the Baton Rouge area, and he had brought his son who was six or seven years old to meet me because he wanted his kid to remember that this was possible.

That also made me realize that I had a responsibility to help other people realize that what I was doing was possible for everyone. Because I didn’t go into this thing with a mission, and I wasn’t there to be a pioneer. I just wanted to go to school. But I realized . . . And I knew that would happen; that it would take on a different meaning for black people because people had come up to me and at home, people would say, “We’re very proud of you,” and things like that, but this was a . . . This man and this little boy . . . That just meant so much to me. It put more responsibility on me because I was trying to figure out how to get out of there. I mean, the experience was so bad. But then, I thought, “Well, I can’t leave because I’ll be disappointing everyone.” It put me in a more . . . It created conflict for me.

I then said to myself, “Well I just can’t leave.” My folks had told me I could leave any time I wanted to. My father said, “You are a person. You’re an individual. Yes, the case is important, but you’re not a case; you’re a person. We love you, and if it gets too rough, you just say you want out, and we’ll get you out.” I just couldn’t figure that . . . I couldn’t do that. I figured I don’t know how I’m going to be able to take it. I then started to feel that I was in a conflictual situation that I couldn’t resolve. I just said, “Time will tell. Something’s got to get better. Something’s got to change, but I shouldn’t go. It sure would be nice to be at Xavier University in New Orleans with all my friends, enjoying themselves, working hard but having a good time, and not be under all this pressure.”

blocks.caption: Ollie H. Burns, profiled in the School of Library and Information Science newsletter, fall 2002.

blocks.body: Ollie H. Burns graduates from the School of Library and Information Science (SLIS).

blocks.caption: The Louisiana Weekly reports the LSU Board of Supervisors’ vote, 1958.

blocks.body: The LSU Board of Supervisors reaffirms its formal policy of segregation.
Freya Anderson Rivers, Oliver Ferlon Mack, Jr., Clifford Ray Smith, et al., successfully sue to attend LSU as undergraduates.

blocks.title: We just kept saying equal
blocks.credit: Freya Anderson Rivers, interviewed by Maxine Crump
blocks.transcript:
FREYA ANDERSON RIVERS: Daddy [Dupuy Anderson] filed suit to integrate LSU. . . The students at Lee High and . . . Most of the high school students, white high school students, think LSU is heaven, and when they found out . . . they were enraged: “Oh, the nigger thinks she’s smart. She can go to LSU now. It wasn’t good enough to just integrate the public schools, now she’s going to LSU. We’ve got to have these coons out at LSU.” All of this crap all over again. So graduating from Lee High didn’t mean anything to me because I knew I had to go through this stuff all over again . . .

MAXINE CRUMP: After all of that at Lee High, why did you decide to go to LSU?

RIVERS: I was on a mission then. It was just a point to prove. You had to go on with it. If I could survive Lee High, I could survive anything. So it wasn’t, it wasn’t fear of anything or . . . I mean, I was just so hard by that time, it just didn’t make me any difference . . .

As Daddy kept saying, he said, “My children don’t have to do this.” He said, “Because I can send them anywhere I want to.” He said, “I’m hoping that we’re opening doors for children that can’t afford to do this, whose only choice might be LSU.” So, that’s what I thought that we were doing.

I was hoping that we were pioneering the way to open the doors for students that would only have this as an alternative, that had, just did not have any other option. That hopefully with an equal educational system, if we were at LSU then maybe they would equalize the facilities at Southern. We just kept saying equal.

RIVERS: The guy from Shreveport spent a lot of time with us because he was living on campus. They trashed his dorm. They broke the windows in the dorm. The police had to come and protect him one night when they started throwing bricks and things through the windows of the dorm. I don’t know if that ever made the paper or not . . .

. . . The Ku Klux Klan came out and burned a cross in front of the library one night about two weeks we after we had been in school. The next morning when we arrived at school the cross was just laying down on the ground in front of the library. The students erected the cross again during the day: “Niggers go home.” It’s so ridiculous because A. P. Tureaud, Jr.[sic] had already integrated the law school, so there were blacks on campus in the law school. Then they had to file suit again and integrate the graduate school at LSU. So there were grad students on campus at LSU. Then, we had to file suit again to integrate the undergrad. I’m willing to bet that LSU is the only university in the country that had three separate suits filed to integrate each division. I know of no other.

CRUMP: How much of what you did do you feel the younger people coming up right behind you knew of what you did? . . .

RIVERS: They didn’t know. Again, as I said, Baton Rouge kept everything quiet, so nobody really knew what we were going through. The adults didn’t know what we were going through, let alone the kids . . . They weren’t forewarned, and it was almost as if each generation that began to come in had to go through it all over again. It wasn’t as severe as what we went through, but they would, every class was breaking ground again. With each new class that came in, every freshman class.

blocks.body: Maxine Crump becomes the first African American to live in an LSU dormitory.

blocks.title: Who was comfortable being where with me
blocks.credit: Maxine Crump, interviewed by Pamela Dean
blocks.transcript:
MAXINE CRUMP: I started becoming aware of who was comfortable being where with me. There were some people who were very comfortable with me in the cafeteria, they were comfortable with me in the dorm, but out on campus in the [Student] Union, they’d pass me like they’d never seen me before. It’s funny, whites often think that the worst thing that can happen to a black is to be yelled a racial slur at. [scoffs] Please, give me racial slurs! Just don’t give me a friend who ignores me in public. A friend who embraced me intimately and then get in public and she’s never seen me before. Give me racial slurs over that.

And then I met Marie Biondo and her sister . . . These were my friends. The Biondos had a Jeep that we would go riding in. A convertible Jeep, which was fun. So I got to do those kind of wild college things. It was like, “Oh, this is being in college!” Riding in a Jeep with the top off of it. Going to get malts; I had never gone to go get malts. My mother was always, “I don’t want you hanging around the malt shop. People are going to say I’m just letting you run wild.” It was like, “I’m running wild! I’m having a malt!” [laughs]

PAMELA DEAN: Where did you go for malts?

CRUMP: At the pharmacist right off of campus. It was a Rexall Drug store, it was called Tiger Town Pharmacy. I remember there seemed to have been a time where there was a question about whether I could sit at the counter. But I did, but they didn’t know I was black because the Italian girls were dark, too. We would go in places where they didn’t know I was black, and they would say, “They don’t know you’re black!” So, a lot of the places I went were like that. A lot.

DEAN: How did you feel about that? Did you think about it at the time?

CRUMP: Yeah. Yeah I did, yeah. I knew that in a way I was passing, but I knew that I wasn’t choosing to pass. I was letting it pass. I wasn’t saying, “I’m going to go in here and pretend to be white.” If anyone had asked me, I would have acknowledged being black, absolutely. I knew that. But what I wanted was the full college experience, and if it meant going in those places they went, then I wanted to go in those places. Because they were college students, not because they were white.

About two years after being there at the university, after they had a large onslaught of blacks come in and blacks couldn’t go into all those places right off campus, then the university issued a statement that said, “You will serve all LSU students or you will move your business.” And then we could go in everywhere. But I was thrown out of one place when I went with some other blacks to a place I had gone to when they didn’t know. And I went in that same place, and it was the Bengal . . . No, the Pastime. They came over immediately and said, “We don’t serve coloreds here.”

DEAN: Was this part of a deliberate attempt to desegregate these places?

CRUMP: It was. I knew what I was doing. I knew that they didn’t accept blacks.

blocks.body: Black students at LSU establish Harambe, a support group with a room of its own on campus.

blocks.title: A bonding group
blocks.transcript:
Harambe was not a radical group. Harambe was a bonding group . . . a support group, maybe. And it really gave us that feeling of family. Could come, we had a room we could come and play our music, people would bring old furniture, okay, and come and sit. But after that there were just ties, we had ties.

It was also a focal point to . . . If you had to make a statement, and Leo [Hamilton] or someone had to represent us, we had a focal point. So it allowed blacks a place to come, which they didn’t have prior to that. And it was sort of a . . . Let’s just say it was a small NAACP version.

blocks.body: Kerry Louis Pourciau was the first African American to be elected president of the LSU Student Government Association (SGA). He later held positions with U.S. Senator Russell Long and New Orleans Mayor Ernest N. Morial. He was economic development director for the City of Baton Rouge and worked in public relations for Gulf States Utilities and the Louisiana Lottery Corporation. Pourciau passed away in 1994. In this clip, Pourciau discusses how his friend, Lora Hinton, was the first African American football player to be recruited for the LSU Tigers.

blocks.title: A new era
blocks.credit: Kerry Pourciau, interviewed by Maxine Crump
blocks.transcript:
KERRY POURCIAU: Well, I think just, you know, looking at racism squarely in the face for what it was, you know: legions of fraternal organizations that didn’t accept blacks, a football team that had actually not had its first black football player by that time. So I was to help usher in, truly, a new era here. To this day, my best friend is the first recruit . . . first black recruit to the LSU football team. That was well over twenty years ago, Lora Hinton. So, I was there and I . . . One thing that I remember about the white kids is that they were open, they were ready, that . . . That Lora walked around as a . . . some god, you know. I mean, and was just so socially advanced anyway that it was a piece of cake for him, really.

MAXINE CRUMP: Well, the history of LSU, ’69 was one of the best years that you could have come, as far as the environment on campus. A lot of movement had taken place in ’68, so you walked into a little bit more openness in the environment.

POURCIAU: Well, I did.

blocks.title: Alpha Kappa Alpha Established at LSU

blocks.caption: Members of Alpha Kappa Alpha at LSU.

blocks.body: With help from the Gamma Eta Omega chapter of Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, Black women at LSU establish a chapter of their own.

blocks.title: Founding the chapter
blocks.transcript:
Well, AKA at Southern [University] helped to get us established at LSU, okay? We had vine sisters from Southern that paired up with each one of us to help us through the process. They were the ones that met with us and talked about how you formulated an organization and all that. So we really have to give credit to Gamma Eta Omega’s chapter because they were the ones that helped to get us started.

We didn’t have rush but we would have . . . I know I remember us having a tea. We all had white dresses and we met in the Union upstairs in one of those rooms.

My job as Dean of Pledges was to outline the activities that we would do. I would plan the social calendar, or the civic calendar, as such. We would do . . . I would get them involved in anything in reference to the Pan-Hellenic council, like the game . . . the football game that’s denoted here. When we got ready to have certain ceremonies that the sorority dictates, you know, I would see to it that they wore the proper attire. I was like the person who was responsible for them . . . the leader who was responsible for them, but they also had their own sponsor. We solicited girls, each one of us would sponsor somebody if we could. But if we sponsored, that really placed an extra responsibility because you had to see to it that they did what they were supposed to do. Plus you had to see to it that they maintained those grades.

We would financially support Sickle Cell, you know, organizations like that, United Way. We would financially support those kinds of things. I remember us going to Hillhaven Rest Home several times, and I remember us doing the Muscular Dystrophy, you know, generating money for that. I remember us helping out with . . . In fact, that’s one of the things that we did when [Kerry] Pourciau ran for SGA [Student Government Association] president [at LSU]. We passed out flyers for that.

blocks.title: LSU Names a Building for A. P. Tureaud, Sr.

blocks.caption: The Daily Reveille reports the building’s dedication, 1990.

blocks.body: The former Classroom Building, at South Stadium Drive and Forestry Lane, is named for civil rights lawyer A. P. Tureaud, Sr.: the first building on LSU’s campus named for a Black person.

pages.title: The 1953 Bus Boycott
pages.lead_caption: An Esso station in Baton Rouge, 1953. Photo courtesy of Ernest Richie.

blocks.body: The city raised bus fares from ten cents to fifteen cents. At that time, 80 percent of bus riders are African American. Reverend T. J. Jemison went to the City-Parish Council to complain about the fare increase and the fact that black people had to stand overcrowded in the back of the bus.

blocks.title: Standing over empty seats
blocks.transcript: The blacks going down into South Baton Rouge were forced to stand up over empty seats. They could put their bags, their bundles in the seat, but they couldn’t put their bodies. And of course I thought that was ridiculous. And I was much younger then and I was more daring and I thought that we had to do something about that. And of course we did.

blocks.title: It was humiliating
blocks.transcript: In some ways, now I can look back on it, it was humiliating for the blacks. Because you get on the bus and you paid what everybody else paid, but you couldn’t sit where everybody else would sit. There was a divided section. You would go to that section and sit on the bus. If you sat anywhere else, you were asked to go to the back of the bus. And it was known in that time that blacks did not sit in the front of the bus.

blocks.body: The City-Parish Council approved Ordinance 222, stating that blacks could fill the bus from the back to the front and whites could fill the bus from front to back on a first-come, first-served seating basis. The ordinance went into effect, but was widely ignored.

blocks.title: First come, first served
blocks.transcript: The City Council heard our plea. They passed an ordinance; the ordinance was Ordinance 222. That said that black people could sit from the back to the front and whites could sit from the front to the back. There would be no reserved seats, and that first come, first served.

blocks.title: June: The strike and the boycott

blocks.body: Bus drivers are ordered to comply with Ordinance 222. A bus driver manhandled a black woman sitting in a front seat of one bus.

blocks.title: The lady on the bus
blocks.transcript: The next morning, a lady got on the bus. And when she got on the bus, the bus driver comes up, took the lady off and tried to arrest her. When the police got there, he arrested the lady. But then somebody came from police headquarters and said “You ain’t got no business arresting this lady.” And he told the policeman, “You go back to headquarters. I’ll handle this.” . . . So the bus company, they got mad and went on a strike.

blocks.body: Reverend Jemison tests the law by sitting in the front seat of a bus. He carries a copy of Ordinance 222 in his shirt pocket.
Two bus drivers are suspended for not complying with Ordinance 222.
Bus drivers strike for four days in response to the enforcement of Ordinance 222.
Raymond Scott announces the bus boycott on radio station WLCS. More than 200 African Americans meet and form the United Defense League (UDL).

blocks.caption: An Esso station in Baton Rouge, 1953. Photo courtesy of Ernest Richie.

blocks.body: Bus drivers end their strike, while African Americans begin a boycott of city buses. The Free Ride System goes into effect.

blocks.title: The night before the boycott
blocks.transcript: The night before the boycott, one little woman asked to speak. She got up and gave a very stirring speech, that she had an old raggedy car, and she would run it until you couldn’t run it any more. That morning at five o’clock we were all in place with our automobiles ready to accept the challenge.

blocks.title: Driving the bus route
blocks.transcript: I would get in my car in the morning, gas it up, and I would go the bus route. The bus went down East Boulevard and went uptown then hit North Boulevard and up. There was a Sears store on the corner there. I would go the bus route and stop. People be on the corners. Get the car loaded and go on up and then come on back out in South Baton Rouge.

blocks.body: June 20: First mass meeting was held at Mt. Zion Baptist Church. Segregationists burned crosses at the church and at Reverend Jemison’s home. June 21: At the second mass meeting, the UDL collected money to purchase gasoline for the car pool. June 22: The third mass meeting is held at Memorial Stadium.

blocks.title: They rode free in the day
blocks.transcript: Well at night, when we had our mass meetings, we would take up money that would pay for the gas and the tires and whatever else happened to the cars during the time they were driving them. The people rode free in the day and paid for it at night.

blocks.title: A show of unity
blocks.transcript: Mass meetings basically took places at churches. When they put on this big mass meeting at Memorial Stadium, that was an effort to show unity, strength, and bring about the raising of funds to finance this massive bus boycott.

blocks.body: Ordinance 251 is passed. This reserved the first two bus seats for white people and the last two for black people. Blacks would fill the bus from back to front and whites from front to back.
Jemison and other black leaders negotiate a compromise (Ordinance 251) with the City-Parish Council thus ending boycott.

blocks.title: Separate but equal was wrong
blocks.transcript: He [Reverend Jemison] went down and entered into a compromise with the mayor and the city council that they wouldn’t desegregate the bus. Jemison thought that was right as long as it was “separate but equal,” because that was the law. There wasn’t any animosity between us. It’s just that I didn’t agree; because to me, “separate but equal” was wrong.

blocks.body: Many objected to the June compromise (including Johnnie Jones, Willis Reed, Dupuy Anderson, Joe Howard and others) and wanted the boycott to continue. Later, Howard was arrested for sitting next to a white man on one of two front seats on a city bus.

blocks.title: My daughter sat in the front
blocks.transcript: My oldest daughter when she got out of high school she had a little summer job working over at Kean’s Laundry. And this was after the boycott, she told me. She got on the bus and she sat in the front. There wasn’t any seats, except some way to the back. And the bus pulled over to the side, and after a while, about five cars of policemen drove up. They got on the bus and asked her, “Why are you sitting here?” She said, “Well, I can sit here.” They made her get in the back.

blocks.body: One of the major differences between the Baton Rouge and Montgomery, Alabama, boycotts is that King went through the Federal Court, whereas Jemison went through the state court. Another key difference is how the white community in Baton Rouge was more flexible than the white community in Montgomery.

blocks.title: The church house and the court house
blocks.credit: Johnnie Jones, civil rights attorney, interviewed by Beth Smith
blocks.transcript:
JOHNNIE JONES: When we prepared the petition for the federal court, and Reverend Jemison did not want that.

BETH SMITH: Why?

JONES: Because he said he wanted the power structure of this city and of this parish to know that we still . . . that the black people still had faith in them and trust them to do right. He was a Christian, you know, that’s religious talk. That was alright in the church house, but that doesn’t mean a thing in the court house. You see? I don’t know if . . . It’s hard to get Martin Luther King, one of the few preachers, and another guy Stalworth I think his name was, out in Alabama, they were one of the few people that saw that difference. That the church house was one thing; the court house was another.

SMITH: Do you think the bus boycott may have been just too soon for Baton Rouge to handle?

JONES: The time had not quite come for Jemison do what Dr. Martin Luther King did, but he did a yeoman’s job, a very good job. He start the ball a-rolling. He got things started. He opened our eyes. Martin Luther King sought out Jemison to get information on how to proceed with a boycott. He was a forerunner. And he . . . His philosophy was filled with good intentions. “Let them see that we still believe that they will do right. We trust them.” And he was hoping. He was hoping that they would go ahead on and desegregate the buses in a different manner. But this with from front to back was what he thought was a step forward. Which it was because you didn’t have to . . . everybody wouldn’t . . . everybody had to stand up at one time or another. And the other one couldn’t tell the other one to move unless the other one being in violation of the law. So it put . . . It put everybody in a position to be in violation of the law. Whereas before Ordinance 222, blacks were always, every time, anytime in violation of the law. If you want to make me so.

pages.title: East Baton Rouge
pages.lead_caption: Marchers on their way to the State Capitol, April 5, 1968.

blocks.body: African Americans organize the Baton Rouge branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). From 1930 to 1955, prominent businessman Benjamin Stanley headed the organization. In 1940, the branch boasted 800 members.
McKinley High School opens, attracting students from around the state. In 1928, the first class of McKinley students graduated.

blocks.title: The hub of education
blocks.credit: Rev. Lionel Lee, teacher and Baptist minister
blocks.transcript: The first and the hub of education was McKinley Senior High School. That was the only school for African Americans. We had kids coming from Clinton, St. Francisville, Port Allen, Brusly, all around [Louisiana] coming to Baton Rouge. There was no other high school for black folks.

blocks.body: Veteran Dupuy Anderson describes his first day on assignment at Ryan Field in Baton Rouge. Reginald Brown recounts his mother’s return from the service.

blocks.title: Ryan Army Air Field
blocks.transcript: I was sent to Ryan Army Air Field as a first lieutenant, Medical Administrative Corps. I went in and had my physical. I went over to the hospital; every typewriter stopped typing. Every head turned toward me. A gray-haired colonel walked out. The captain gave him my papers; he threw them back to me, said, “They must have made a mistake.” I took my papers and I went home. Took off my uniform; I felt like burning it.

blocks.title: Home from the war
blocks.transcript: See, my mother, she was a veteran of World War II, and so was her brother, my uncle. When they came back to Baton Rouge from the war, it was very, very much a crude awakening for her. She thought things would be a lot different.

blocks.body: After several Boy Scouts drowned in the Mississippi River, the Reverend W. K. Brooks launched a fund-raising drive to build a swimming pool for African American children. The Baton Rouge Recreation and Parks Commission (now BREC) then operated swimming pools for whites only. Once completed, the black community turned their new pool over to the Parks Commission.

blocks.title: Tax time
blocks.transcript: I can remember Daddy [Leo Stanley Butler] would get grumpy during tax time; we had to pay income tax and tax to the city. And why is it, if he was paying tax, [we] could not go to swim in that pool? And rather than have us integrate that pool, they closed it.

blocks.body: Park officials denied use of the city’s golf courses to six African Americans: Malcolm Lagarde, Willie Major, Wesley Nicholas, Allen White, Roosevelt Spencer and Alvin Scott. The six retained attorneys Johnnie Jones and Bruce Bell and filed suit to integrate the golf courses. In response, the Parks Commission built a course in a predominantly black neighborhood. The suit remained mired in the court system for nearly a decade.

blocks.title: A black golf course
blocks.transcript: I objected [to] raising money to build a black swimming pool. I lost out. When we got a golf course, we had a suit pending; we had a federal judge that was not in favor of integrating. They hurriedly built a black golf course, nine holes. I objected to that. I was invited to the dedication, but I did not go.

blocks.body: Nearly two months after lunch counter sit-ins in Greensboro, North Carolina, eight Southern University students staged a sit-in at Kress Department Store. The following day, nine more students sat in at various locations in the city. Police arrested all of the protesters for disturbing the peace.

blocks.title: At the lunch counters
blocks.credit: Eula Mae Hatter, WXOK radio announcer
blocks.transcript: Students who tried to be served at these lunch counters; they would be turned down and told to leave the stores. And there were times when they didn’t leave, and they would go to jail. But, this was at the beginning of some of the unpleasantness that happened in the late fifties and sixties.

blocks.caption: Southern University students on their way to a mass meeting, carrying signs that read “Old Ways No More.” Newspaper photo by Bob Wall, March 30, 1960.

blocks.body: Thousands of students marched from Southern University to the State Capitol in support of their jailed comrades. University President Felton Clark expelled the sit-in participants and closed the campus.
Students at Southern University organized a Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) chapter. In December, members of the Baton Rouge chapter of CORE staged a series of sit-ins.

blocks.title: We were willing
blocks.transcript: We were a little apprehensive. We really didn’t know what they were going to do. During the sit-ins, sometimes you might get beat, sometimes they’d pour coffee on you, or anything. We had no idea what they might do to us. But we were willing to do whatever we needed to do to bring it to the attention of the nation, I guess you might say.

blocks.body: A state court convicted sit-in participants of disturbing the peace and sentenced them to four-month jail terms. In December 1961, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling in their case (Garner v. Louisiana) and declared that their convictions violated the right to due process guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment. It was the only sit-in case to receive a favorable ruling by the Court.
Police arrested twenty-five members of CORE, all Southern University students, for picketing downtown stores. All refused bail.

Nearly 4,000 students marched to the parish prison in support of the 25 jailed CORE members. National CORE representative, Reverend B. Elton Cox led a peaceful rally outside, but authorities ordered the crowd to disperse and then fired teargas. Police arrested Cox and charged him with inciting a riot. Convicted in State Court, he appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court and his case, Cox v. Louisiana, led to a landmark ruling upholding the right of peaceful protest.
Southern University expelled seven student activists. Fearing mass demonstrations, SU President Felton Clark closed campus.
NAACP Youth Director Pearl George led a group of African Americans to swim in the white-only City Park pool.

blocks.title: The swimming pools were not integrated
blocks.credit: Debra George, daughter of Pearl George
blocks.transcript: I remember when we had gone to City Park—the swimming pools were not integrated—and we went there to swim. Once we had gotten there, the people at the pool that worked there started getting all the whites out of the pool and telling them to leave, because we were getting ready to go to the back to shower, to come back out and get into the pool. But by that time the police had rushed in, and they escorted us out.

blocks.body: Inez Anderson, wife of Dupuy Anderson, describes persistent and personal attacks against their family’s home during her husband’s multi-pronged fight for equality.

blocks.title: They shot in our house
blocks.transcript:
Oh, my goodness. They shot in our house. We had a big picture glass window in the front. We had all this . . . Whenever he’d be home, we would all get together because the kids were glad to see him. We would have dinner. We were in the dining room. We got up. He was leaving going to another meeting. When we got up and left out of the dining room, we heard this big crash. Somebody had . . . we went back in there. There was a hole in the picture glass window. It was a bullet hole. Of course, he went on to his meeting [laughs].

We called the police. Of course, they came on out and everything, but they never could find anything. Now, here’s a big bullet hole. It had ricocheted up the wall, up the glass. Oh, they couldn’t find anything. They were so sorry. They were going to put more protection out there. Of course, they didn’t, but nevertheless. That was one thing.

Then again, there was a cross burned on our lawn one night. Every weekend during the summertime . . . Have you ever tried to wash egg off of concrete when it’s ninety-something degrees? You had to scrape it up. This is what I had to go through; sometimes during the week, but mostly on the weekends. Evidently they’d come down the driveway because the house was set back a little bit. They would throw eggs at the front door. Our front entrance would just be plastered with eggs. Of course, as we say, “It was horrible.” Every time he was involved in, like when he was running for mayor, or if he had a court case coming up, or whatever, it would get worse. All of this stuff would just get worse. I was the one who had to get up there and scrape it up because you couldn’t wash it up. It wouldn’t wash up. You had to scrape it.

Then, we had as I said this cross burning. They sent two FBI [Federal Bureau of Investigation] agents out after all of this. When they came, they were two of the biggest men I’d ever seen in my life. I had to look up at them. When they came out, I was . . . I had just had it. I don’t know where I got the courage to talk to them the way I did, but I told them. I said, “Okay, they shot in my house. They throw eggs on my house. I’m tired of scraping the egg off of my house. They’re burning a cross.” I said, “I’m telling you right now. My husband has bought me a gun and I am being trained to use it.” Which was the truth. I said, “I may not have to call you anymore. Because if I catch anybody throwing eggs at my house, I’m going to shoot. If I catch anybody burning a cross on my lawn, I’m going to shoot. There won’t be any point in you coming here because I will have taken care of it.”

blocks.body: Twelve downtown Baton Rouge department stores integrated their lunch counters after negotiations with the Biracial Committee, created by Mayor Jack Christian the previous May.
Fearing court-ordered integration, the Parks Commission closed City Park swimming pool.
A sniper assassinated Martin Luther King, Jr. in Memphis, Tennessee.

blocks.caption: The march to the State Capitol, April 5, 1968.
Marchers on their way to the State Capitol, April 5, 1968.

blocks.body: Students marched from Southern University to the State Capitol mourning King’s murder. SU President Felton Clark closed campus to prevent further protests.
African Americans firebombed several white-owned businesses in Baton Rouge.
Fearing black citizens were planning a riot, Baton Rouge Mayor Woody Dumas ordered a voluntary curfew to begin at dusk.

Police officers shot and killed two African Americans within a matter of days. Their deaths led to marches, pickets, and small-scale rioting. Mayor Dumas placed Baton Rouge under a curfew and Governor John McKeithen mobilized the National Guard.

blocks.title: The summer of 1969
blocks.credit: Paul Burns, LSU forestry professor and president of the Baton Rouge Council on Human Relations
blocks.transcript: The summer of 1969, there were four males, young black males, who were killed by the police in Baton Rouge. Shot in the back. I think they were, all of them, unarmed. The local police were just shooting black people in the back! They claimed they were burglary suspects, and I wouldn’t be surprised if they had committed burglary, but they had no chance to defend themselves because they were killed.

blocks.body: Black Muslims and the police engaged in a deadly confrontation in downtown Baton Rouge. The conflict ended with the deaths of two police officers, two Black Muslims, and injury to thirty-nine others.
Sheriff’s deputies killed two Southern University students taking part in a rally to protest conditions at the school.

blocks.title: The deputies lined up
blocks.transcript: It was a student protest. I was working on the campus in that building, and I was standing in the front of that building when the sheriff’s deputies lined up. I don’t remember how many. It may have been thirty, forty, fifty; I don’t remember. But they all lined up and then they were standing in front of the kids and they pointed their rifles. I was standing right on that corner, and then all of a sudden, gun shots were fired and tear gas was fired. Folks just went running. We could see the two students laying on the ground, and they laid there some time. I don’t know if they could have been saved or not, but had they maybe been given immediate attention, they may have survived.

pages.title: The Nation
pages.lead_caption: The Plessy v. Ferguson marker in New Orleans, written by historian Keith Weldon Medley for the Crescent City Peace Alliance and placed at Press Street and the railroad yards on February 12, 2009.

blocks.caption: The Plessy v. Ferguson marker in New Orleans, written by historian Keith Weldon Medley for the Crescent City Peace Alliance and placed at Press Street and the railroad yards on February 12, 2009.

blocks.body: The U.S. Supreme Court legitimized the principle of “separate but equal” in its Plessy v. Ferguson decision, beginning the Jim Crow era.

World War II (1939–1945) saw more than 100 million people serving in military units with either the Allied or Axis powers. During American involvement in the war, the number of enlisted African Americans rose from a few thousand to over one million by war’s end. Serving in segregated units in every theater, African Americans fought bravely and with distinction, while simultaneously struggling for their own civil rights at home. Although the Armed Forces’ policy of segregation continued until 1948, World War II laid the foundation for the integration of the military.

The Korean War (1950–1953) began nearly five years after Japan’s World War II surrender in September 1945. American administrators divided the Korean Peninsula (long ruled by Japan) along the 38th Parallel. U.S. forces occupied the southern half of the country, the Republic of Korea, while Soviet forces occupied the northern half, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. In June 1950, North Korean forces invaded the South and refused to withdraw, compelling President Harry Truman to authorize the utilization of the U.S. Armed Forces. As in World War II, enlisted African Americans served in Korea in all capacities. The disbanding of the historic all-black 24th Infantry Regiment during the war signified the end of segregation in the military.

The Vietnam War (1956–1975) was fought between communist North Vietnam (supported by China and its allies) and the government of South Vietnam (supported by the United States and its allies). American involvement in the war was designed in part to prevent a communist takeover of South Vietnam, thus the war was a proxy conflict of the Cold War. The Vietnam War saw the highest enlistment of African Americans and marked the first fully integrated deployment of U.S. troops. During the height of the war, over 12% of service members were African American.

The Civil Rights Act of 1964, the nation’s benchmark civil rights legislation, prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, skin color, religion, sex or national origin. Passage of the Act ended the application of “Jim Crow” laws, which had been upheld by the Supreme Court in the 1896 case Plessy v. Ferguson.

The Voting Rights Act of 1965, signed into law by President Lyndon B. Johnson, bans racial discrimination in voting practices by the federal government as well as by state and local governments. Designed to enforce the voting rights guaranteed by the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, Congress later amended the Act five times to expand its protections.

The Relentless Pursuit of “Equal”: Integrating LSU was a gallery exhibition in the Hill Memorial Library Lecture Hall from January 21 to March 29, 2014, commemorating the 50th anniversary of the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. It traces the evolution of LSU from an institution embracing an official policy of racial segregation to one actively promoting the concept that “cultural inclusion at LSU is paramount to the success of the university.” The exhibition was timed to correspond with Created Equal: America’s Civil Rights Struggle, a film-based public program funded by the National Endowment for the Humanities and hosted by LSU Libraries in the spring of 2014.

Its listening station, funded by the Williams Center Endowment, featured an interactive timeline with oral history clips from those who integrated LSU, alongside timelines of other civil rights activities in the Baton Rouge area that put the events at the university in context. Interview clips and other materials offer personal, eyewitness narratives of the 1953 Baton Rouge bus boycott, of breaking color barriers on the LSU campus in the 1950s and 1960s, and of East Baton Rouge civil rights activities from the 1950s through the 1970s.

LSU Libraries Special Collections welcomes donations of original materials, such as letters, photographs, oral histories or ephemera, that help build a more complete and inclusive record of this era in the Libraries’ collections.

All oral history interviews from which excerpts were taken are housed with the T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History and are part of the Louisiana and Lower Mississippi Valley Collections, LSU Libraries Special Collections, Baton Rouge, Louisiana. For citation information for each interview, please contact the Williams Center. Some of the interviews are online in the Center’s Civil Rights Collection on the Louisiana Digital Library.

Old Ways No More

Middleton Library also showcased “Old Ways No More,” a web-based production featuring oral histories and other sources from LSU Libraries Special Collections that document the Baton Rouge bus boycott of 1953, its antecedents and its aftereffects. It features audio clips from the McKinley High School Oral History Series and others within the Williams Center Civil Rights Collection, and was offered as a precursor to Created Equal. “Old Ways” debuted at the 2003 academic conference held at Southern University in honor of the boycott’s 50th anniversary. The work is based largely on the research conducted by Dr. Mary Price for her dissertation, “Beyond Black and White: The Civil Rights Movement in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, 1945–1972.” The presentation was produced by Matthew Mullenix and Mary Price.

Acknowledgments

The exhibition was curated by Leah Wood Jewett, Exhibitions Coordinator; Barry Cowan, Assistant Archivist, University Archives; and Jennifer A. Cramer, Director, T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History. The physical exhibition was designed and installed by Leah Wood Jewett, with assistance from Louise Cheetham, Graduate Assistant, Exhibitions. The listening station was built by Kyle Tanglao, Williams Center Audio Engineer and Web Developer, with TimelineJS from Northwestern University.

Several individuals helped make this exhibition possible. The curators wish to thank Erin Hess, Williams Center Manuscript Processor; Kitty Pheney, LSU School of Art, and her students Virginia Patterson, Melody Reah and Andre Charitat; and Mary Price and Matt Mullenix, former Williams Center staff. We appreciate the help of many other staff members throughout the stages of planning and installation.
